newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: CRICKET-TAYLOR UNLIKELY ALLY FOR BELEAGURED ATHERTON.
newsitem.headline: CRICKET-TAYLOR UNLIKELY ALLY FOR BELEAGURED ATHERTON.

text.p: Beleaguered England captain Mike Atherton has found an unlikely ally in his Australian counterpart Mark Taylor.
Both opening batsmen, currently struggling for runs at any level, are fighting to keep their jobs for this year's six-test Ashes series in England.
While Atherton's form has declined gradually over the past year, Taylor's troubles have suddenly engulfed him.
Unchallenged as leader and opener at the start of the current test series against West Indies, Taylor acknowledges a prolonged form slump has placed his future as captain under scrutiny.
"Being a captain, I know what Mike is going through because I have some experience of it myself this year," Taylor said in an interview.
Taylor, 32, a veteran of 76 tests and with 14 test centuries to his name, has scored a paltry 381 runs in 20 innings in all forms of cricket in Australia this season.

Averaging only 19, Taylor has just one half century to his credit in that time, a factor in Australia's failure to qualify for the final of the annual triangular competition on home soil for the first time in 17 years.
The test arena has offered no respite. In six test innings against the pace battery of Curtly Ambrose and company, his highest score is 43.
In public, Taylor has become increasingly frustrated by the media's reaction to his dip in form, an experience he feels sure is shared by Atherton.

"People say 'why did you play that shot', 'why are you doing this or that'. It just happens that way. You can try and work and work and work to try to avoid doing it, but it's the pressure of the game, the bowling.
"People almost assume that you are incompetent. That's when you sit at a press conference and look at a guy very hard who is asking the question and feel like belting him."
Yet despite Taylor's poor form, his team lead the series 2-1 heading into the fourth test in Adelaide, starting on Saturday, with a final showdown in Perth in early February.
Asked whether his position in the side was at risk if he added to a run of low scores in Adelaide and Perth, Taylor replied: "I don't know."
"That is a question you will have to ask the selectors. At this stage, I have had only positive vibes from the selectors that my place is not in jeopardy. Only time will tell.
"If you look at the past...I'm not Robinson Crusoe (alone) in this, a lot of captains have done it.

"Every captain has a lean patch at some stage -- Greg Chappell had a lean trot, Allan Border had some lean trots. That's when, I suppose, the captain gets a bit of extra leeway. He may get a few more games than someone else.
"I've always considered myself to be a bit of an optimist and there is no way on earth that I'm going to write this summer off."
"If Mark Taylor walks out and makes a hundred in Adelaide...then suddenly it's been a good summer.

"If Australia win in Adelaide and we win the Frank Worrell trophy, then all of a sudden all is forgotten. The other option is that Mark Taylor doesn't make any runs and we still win and I'd still be happy, although of course I'd like to bat well."
The third possibility is that Taylor fails again with the bat and Australia lose, a scenario that the left-hander has not considered, at least publicly.
And with West Indies buoyant after their decisive win in the third test in Melbourne, such a possibility appears increasingly plausible.
Immediately after the cessation of hostilities in Perth, Australia fly to South Africa for a three-test series.
From there it is on to England for the six-test Ashes series. At the moment it remains anyone's guess whether it will be Taylor and Atherton tossing the coin before the first test at Edgbaston.
